overview: This unit covers Java methods (Methode), parameters (Parameter), return values (Rückgabewert), and passing arrays. Java always copies the argument value when a method is called; for arrays, that value is the reference (Referenz), so changes to elements can be visible. Insertion Sort creates a sorted copy by inserting values one at a time into a sorted prefix (sortiertes Präfix). The order of the conditions ensures valid array accesses, the insertion position preserves stability (Stabilität), and the presented variant has quadratic runtime (Laufzeit).

entries.short: A method is a named, reusable block of code that encapsulates a task.
entries.explanation: A method groups statements under a name so they can be called deliberately and reused. Methods help break a problem into smaller subtasks. They can accept input values and return a value, or return no result value as `void`.
entries.example: A method `min` can determine the smallest value in an array.
pitfalls: A method is executed only when it is called.
entries.heading: 1. Methoden

entries.short: A method definition specifies, among other things, the return type, name, parameters, and body.
entries.explanation: In `public static int[] readArray(int number) { ... return result; }`, `public` and `static` indicate visibility and invocation style, `int[]` is the return type, and `readArray` is the method name. The parameters appear in parentheses, and the body contains the statements. A `return` statement ends the call and, for a method with a return type, supplies the specified value.
entries.example: `int min(int[] b) { ... return result; }` defines a method that accepts an array and returns an `int`.
pitfalls: The return type specifies the type of the value returned.
entries.heading: Aufbau

entries.short: The formal parameter appears in the method definition; the actual argument is the specific value supplied in the call.
entries.explanation: A formal parameter is a variable through which a method receives an input value, such as `int[] b` in `min(int[] b)`. The actual argument is the value the caller supplies in the call, such as `a` in `min(a)`. When the method is called, the argument value is copied into the parameter.
entries.example: In `min(a)`, `b` is the formal parameter and `a` is the actual argument.
pitfalls: Parameter and argument refer to different locations in a program.
related: Value Copying on a Method Call
entries.heading: Begriffe

entries.short: A local variable exists only within the block in which it is declared.
entries.explanation: A local variable is declared inside a method or another block and is available there. Local variables with the same name in different methods are independent of one another. Therefore, `result` in `main` and `result` in `min` are two different variables.
entries.example: In `int result = min(a);`, `result` in `main` is initialized with the return value only after `min` returns.
pitfalls: Having the same name does not mean that two variables refer to the same memory location.
entries.heading: Begriffe

entries.short: A `void` method returns no value and is also called a procedure.
entries.explanation: The return type `void` indicates that a method call produces no result value. Such a method can still execute statements and, for example, modify an array or produce output. It finishes execution without returning a value.
entries.example: `public static void setFirst(int[] b) { b[0] = 9; }` is a `void` method.
pitfalls: `void` does not mean that the method has no effect.
entries.heading: Begriffe

entries.short: A precondition must hold before a method can be called correctly.
entries.explanation: A precondition describes what requirements the input must meet for the method to perform its task. The method `min` reads `b[0]` at the start, so the array passed to it must contain at least one element. This access would be invalid for an empty array.
entries.example: For `min(b)`, `b.length > 0` must hold.
pitfalls: A precondition is not automatically guaranteed by the method name.
entries.heading: Begriffe

entries.short: `main(String[] args)` is the program entry point, and the words after the class name are stored as strings in `args`.
entries.explanation: Java starts the program at the appropriate `main` method. The words supplied when the program starts are stored as elements in the `args` array, beginning at index `0`. Each element is a string and must be converted to another data type if needed.
entries.example: When started with `java Test Hel lo World!`, `args[0]`, `args[1]`, and `args[2]` contain the strings `"Hel"`, `"lo"`, and `"World!"`.
pitfalls: The class name itself is not an element of `args`.
entries.heading: und Kommandozeilenargumente

entries.short: A control-flow diagram represents program execution as nodes and directed arrows.
entries.explanation: Nodes represent statements, decisions, start, and end, for example; arrows show which steps may follow one another. Each method can be represented as a separate subdiagram. A method call can appear as its own node, connected to the flow of the called method.
entries.example: In the diagram for `min`, a true loop test leads to the comparison `b[i] < result`; a false test ends the loop.
pitfalls: A method call is not the same as the entire control flow of the called method.
entries.heading: Kontrollflussdiagramm

entries.short: A call executes the called method; on return, execution resumes at the waiting call with its result.
entries.explanation: On a call, execution in the caller is suspended and the called method starts with its own local variables. When it reaches `return`, that call ends and execution continues after the call site. In `int result = min(a);`, `result` is initialized only after the method returns.
entries.example: If `min(a)` returns the value `2`, `result` in `main` is then set to `2` and `write(result)` is executed.
pitfalls: The caller executes the statement after the call only once the method call has finished.
entries.heading: Call und Return für

entries.term: Value Copying on a Method Call
entries.short: Java always passes arguments by copying their values.
entries.explanation: When a method is called, each formal parameter receives a copy of the value of the actual argument. For a primitive type, this is the primitive value; for an array, it is the value of the array reference. Therefore, the method cannot reassign the caller's variable by changing its parameter.
entries.example: After `int n = 2; zero(n);`, `n` remains `2`, even if `zero` sets the parameter `number` to `0`.
pitfalls: Even for arrays, the reference is copied; the caller's variable is not passed.
entries.heading: Basistyp: Die Methode bekommt eine Kopie

entries.short: A primitive type stores a primitive value, such as an integer, directly in a variable.
entries.explanation: When a primitive type is passed, the primitive value is copied into the formal parameter. A later assignment to the parameter therefore does not change the caller's variable. `int` is an example of a primitive type.
entries.example: In `int n = 2; zero(n);`, `number = 0` in `zero` does not change the variable `n`.
pitfalls: Changing the parameter value does not change the caller's variable.
related: Value Copying on a Method Call
entries.heading: Basistyp: Die Methode bekommt eine Kopie

entries.short: An array reference is the value a program uses to access an array.
entries.explanation: A variable of type `int[]` contains a reference to an array, not the array's elements themselves. When this reference is copied, the original variable and the copy can reach the same array. Changes to elements can therefore be visible through both variables.
entries.example: After `int[] b = a;`, `a` and `b` refer to the same array.
pitfalls: Copying an array reference does not create a new array.
related: Value Copying on a Method Call
entries.heading: Übersicht

entries.short: Changing an element affects the shared array, while reassigning the parameter changes only its local reference copy.
entries.explanation: If `b` and `a` refer to the same array, `b[0] = 9` changes the array that is also accessible through `a`. By contrast, `b = new int[2]` changes only what the local variable `b` refers to. The caller's variable `a` still points to the original array.
entries.example: `setFirst(a)` with `b[0] = 9` changes `a[0]`; `replace(a)` with `b = new int[2]` leaves `a` unchanged.
pitfalls: Assigning to a parameter does not reassign the caller's variable.
entries.heading: Übersicht

entries.short: Aliasing occurs when multiple variables refer to the same array.
entries.explanation: With aliasing, two or more variables access the same array. A change to an element through one of these variables is therefore also visible when accessed through the others. This results from shared references.
entries.example: After `int[] b = a;`, an assignment such as `b[0] = 9` is also visible through `a[0]`.
pitfalls: Two variables with the same contents do not necessarily point to the same array.
entries.heading: Übersicht

entries.short: A true array copy is created by allocating a new array and copying each element into it.
entries.explanation: First, allocate a new array with the same length as the original. Then copy each element from the original to the same index in the new array and return a reference to the new array. The new array is independent of the original, so changes to its elements do not change the original.
entries.example: For `a = {7, 2}`, `copy(a)` creates a new array `{7, 2}`; then `b[0] = 9` can be executed without changing `a[0]`.
pitfalls: `int[] b = a` copies only the reference, not the array.
entries.heading: Echte Kopie erstellen

entries.short: Insertion Sort sorts values by inserting each input value into an already sorted prefix.
entries.explanation: The method shown creates a new array `b` with the same length as the input `a`. It traverses the input from left to right and, for each index `i`, inserts the value `a[i]` at its sorted position in `b[0..i]`. At the end, it returns `b`, leaving the input unchanged and producing a sorted copy.
entries.example: The input `a = {3, 1, 2}` produces `b = {1, 2, 3}`.
pitfalls: The implementation shown in the lecture searches for the insertion position from left to right.
entries.heading: 4. Insertion Sort

entries.short: A sorted prefix is the already ordered leading part of an array.
entries.explanation: As Insertion Sort traverses the input, `b[0..i-1]` contains the values processed so far in sorted order before `a[i]` is inserted. After the insertion, `b[0..i]` is sorted. Thus, the prefix grows by one element in each iteration.
entries.example: Before the next value is inserted into `{1, 3, 7, 9}`, this array is the sorted prefix.
pitfalls: The prefix refers only to the already processed leading entries, not necessarily to the entire array.
entries.heading: Zerlegung in Teilprobleme

entries.short: An insertion finds the new value's position, shifts the following values to the right, and writes the value into the free position.
entries.explanation: Use `locate` to determine the insertion position `j` for `x` in the sorted prefix `b[0..i-1]`. Use `shift` to move the values `b[j..i-1]` one position to the right. Then write `x` to `b[j]`; this way, `b[0..i]` contains the same previous values plus `x` in sorted order.
entries.example: When inserting `5` into `{1, 3, 7, 9}`, `j = 2`; after shifting and writing, the result is `{1, 3, 5, 7, 9}`.
pitfalls: The value must be written to `b[j]` only after the shift.
entries.heading: Ablauf einer Einfügung

entries.short: `locate` searches the sorted prefix for the insertion position of a new value.
entries.explanation: The method starts with `j = 0` and increments `j` while `j < i` and `x >= b[j]` hold. It then returns `j`. The result is the first position where the new value can stand before a larger existing value; for equal values, the search moves past them.
entries.example: For `b = {1, 3, 7, 9}`, `x = 5`, and `i = 4`, `locate` returns index `2`.
pitfalls: The search range ends exclusively at `i`.
entries.heading: Code

entries.short: `shift` moves the values from `b[j..i-1]` one position to the right.
entries.explanation: Set `k` to `i - 1`. While `k >= j`, copy `b[k]` to `b[k + 1]` and decrement `k`. This frees position `j`, where the new value can then be written.
entries.example: With `j = 2` and `i = 4`, first `b[3]` is copied to `b[4]`, then `b[2]` is copied to `b[3]`.
pitfalls: The loop must also process `k = j` to free the insertion position.
related: Why shift Proceeds from Right to Left
entries.heading: Code

entries.term: Why shift Proceeds from Right to Left
entries.short: Shifting from right to left copies each value before its original position is overwritten.
entries.explanation: When shifting to the right, the source and destination ranges overlap. Starting on the right copies the last required value to its destination before that destination overwrites another required value. Shifting from left to right could lose values before they are copied.
entries.example: To shift `7` and `9` one position in `{1, 3, 7, 9, 0}`, first copy `9` from index `3` to `4`, then `7` from `2` to `3`.
pitfalls: Copying from left to right can destroy source data when ranges overlap.
entries.heading: Warum von rechts nach links schieben?

entries.short: With `&&`, the right operand is not evaluated if the left operand is false.
entries.explanation: In `j < i && x >= b[j]`, `j < i` is checked first. If `j < i` is false, the comparison with `b[j]` is skipped. In particular, when `j = i`, `b[i]` is not read.
entries.example: For `j = i`, `j < i` is false, so `x >= b[j]` is not evaluated.
pitfalls: If the conditions were reversed, `b[j]` could be read before the index check.
entries.heading: Short-Circuit bei

entries.short: A sorting algorithm is stable if elements with equal keys retain their original relative order.
entries.explanation: `locate` uses `x >= b[j]`, so it moves past equal values that have already been inserted. The new value of equal size is inserted after them. Thus, elements with equal sort keys retain their order from the input.
entries.example: When sorting people by age, two people of the same age retain their original order with a stable algorithm.
pitfalls: If `x >= b[j]` is replaced by `x > b[j]`, the new equal value can end up before the existing ones.
entries.heading: Stabilität durch

entries.short: The presented Insertion Sort variant requires a quadratic number of steps in the number of elements.
entries.explanation: In iteration `i`, `locate` takes approximately `j` steps and `shift` takes exactly `i - j` copy steps; together, that is approximately `i` steps. Summing over all insertions gives $$\sum_{i=1}^{n-1} i = 1 + 2 + \dots + (n-1) = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} \in \Theta(n^2).$$ Quadratic growth means that, for large `n`, doubling the input size causes approximately four times as much work.
pitfalls: The formula counts the work approximately; it is not an exact count of every machine operation.
entries.heading: 6. Kosten

entries.short: Helper methods structure the code, and the JVM can reduce call costs through inlining.
entries.explanation: Breaking the code into small methods such as `locate` and `shift` makes individual tasks clearer. A method call can incur additional work, called call overhead. The JVM can replace a call with the method body; this optimization is called inlining.
entries.example: At an appropriate point, the JVM can replace a call to `locate(b, x, i)` directly with the code of `locate`.
pitfalls: Inlining is a JVM optimization and does not change the program's meaning.
entries.heading: Helfer oder alles in einer Methode?

entries.short: An invariant is a statement that holds at a specified point in every iteration.
entries.explanation: For Insertion Sort, the central invariant after insertion in iteration `i` is: `b[0..i]` is sorted and contains exactly the first `i + 1` values of the input. It describes both the order of the values and the fact that no processed input value has been lost or added. The invariant is used to justify the algorithm's correctness.
entries.example: After inserting `a[2]`, `b[0..2]` is sorted and contains exactly `a[0]`, `a[1]`, and `a[2]`.
pitfalls: Sorted order alone is not enough; the invariant must also specify which values are present.
entries.heading: 7. Korrektheit

entries.short: After the last iteration, the result array is a sorted copy of the input.
entries.explanation: Before the first insertion, the empty prefix is sorted. In each iteration, the algorithm inserts the next input value at the position found and shifts existing values without losing them; thus, the invariant continues to hold for the longer prefix. For `i = n - 1`, the prefix covers the entire result array, which is therefore sorted and contains exactly the input values.
entries.example: For the input `{3, 1, 2}`, `sort` returns a new array `{1, 2, 3}`.
pitfalls: A correctly sorted result must also contain the same values as the input.
entries.heading: 7. Korrektheit
